summary: This memo specifies a method for sending IP multicast datagrams over Token-Ring local area networks. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending one message to a group of computers on a ring-shaped network needs special handling. This paper explains how. It is historic.

questions: how does multicast work on token ring
subtitle: Transmitting group messages over ring-shaped local networks

tldr.problem: IP multicast allows one sender to transmit to a group of receivers by using special group addresses. Token-Ring local area networks have a different hardware addressing scheme than Ethernet, with support for only 31 special functional addresses, making it challenging to support multicast efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: All IP multicast traffic on a Token-Ring is mapped to a single functional address (03-00-00-20-00-00 in canonical form). Hosts must configure their network interface to accept frames sent to this address and then check the IP header to determine if the frame is relevant to them.
tldr.outcome: This simple approach works but causes all multicast frames on the ring to be delivered to all hosts, requiring software filtering. The RFC is Historic because Token-Ring networks are obsolete and no longer widely deployed.

today: RFC 1469 is Historic. Token-Ring networks have become obsolete and are no longer in use. Modern networks use Ethernet, which handles multicast more efficiently. This RFC is retained for historical reference and for anyone maintaining legacy Token-Ring systems.

sections.title: Multicast on Local Networks
sections.content:
IP multicast allows one computer to send a single message to a group of recipients rather than either sending individual copies to each one (unicast) or broadcasting to everyone on the network (broadcast). Multicast addresses are a special range called Class D addresses, from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255.

For multicast to work on a local area network (LAN), these IP addresses must be translated into hardware addresses that the network interface can understand. On Ethernet and FDDI networks, this mapping is straightforward. Token-Ring networks, however, use a different addressing scheme with special limitations that make multicast more complex to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: IP multicast is like writing an email to a mailing list instead of individual people. But Token-Ring networks need special hardware tricks to make this work, and there are only a few tricks available.

sections.title: Token-Ring Addressing
sections.content:
Token-Ring networks support three types of addresses: individual addresses (sent to one computer, like unicast), group addresses (sent to multiple computers, like multicast), and functional addresses (reserved for standard functions like bridge traffic or network management).

Functional addresses are indicated by special bit patterns in the hardware address. A Token-Ring address is 6 octets (48 bits). When both the I/G bit (individual/group) and the U/L bit (universal/local) are set, the address is a functional address, marked by a Functional Address Indicator (FAI) bit set to 0. There are only 31 possible functional addresses, shared among all protocols on the network.

The problem: Ethernet and FDDI can create unique hardware multicast addresses for thousands of IP multicast groups using the lower 23 bits of the multicast address, but Token-Ring's 31 functional addresses are too few for this approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Token-Ring has only 31 special addresses reserved for group messages, but there could be thousands of different groups. So all IP multicast groups must share one address, and computers have to read the actual message to know if it is for them.

sections.title: The Solution
sections.content:
RFC 1469 recommends mapping all IP multicast addresses to a single Token-Ring functional address: 03-00-00-20-00-00 in canonical form (the bit order used in standards documents) or C0-00-00-04-00-00 in non-canonical form (the bit order used by Token-Ring hardware in memory).

When a Token-Ring interface is configured for multicast, it sets its hardware address filter to accept frames destined to this functional address. However, because this address may be shared with other protocols, the receiving software must examine the IP header to determine if the frame is an IP multicast frame intended for the receiving host's group memberships. The RFC notes that different bridges or ring segments may use different mapping methods if needed, and backward compatibility requires systems to also support the less efficient method of using the all-rings broadcast address.
sections.plainLanguage: All IP multicast messages on a Token-Ring are addressed to one special hardware address. The network card accepts all messages sent to that address, and the software looks inside each message to see if it was meant for that particular computer.
